newsitem.title: ITALY: Generali says not liable for Holocaust claims.
newsitem.headline: Generali says not liable for Holocaust claims.

text.p: Italian insurer Assicurazioni Generali said on Friday that reports that it could be liable for tens of thousands of life insurance claims by descendants of Holocaust victims were groundless.

The Financial Times reported last month that Generali was being pressed by Yad Vashem, the Israeli-based Holocaust research institute, to open files on possibly tens of thousands of former customers who were murdered by the Nazis in central and eastern Europe.
It said release of the files could open the door for a flood of claims against Generali by Holocaust victims and their descendants who have not received proceeds from policies.
"There is no basis for the statement relating to "tens of thousands" of policies, as erroneously reported," Generali said in a statement which did not refer specifically to any one press report.
Generali said "with the exception of a few isolated cases, where there are detailed indications, it is almost impossible to verify the existence of single, specific policies."
The company said it was prepared to throw open its records at its headquarters in the North-eastern port of Trieste but it was not willing to recognise any legal liability.

"Generali is willing to agree on a procedure for an examination of its records in Trieste which would enable an agreed, acceptable body to identify Jewish policy holders in Central and Eastern Europe in (the) time period preceding World War Two," the statement said.

Generali's proposed takeover of Israeli insurer Leumi Insurance Holdings is being held up while Israeli officials determine whether the Italian firm is liable for life insurance claims by Holocaust victims and their descendants.
Generali said that its businesses in central and eastern Europe were seized by communist governments in the 1940s.

"Generali was initially ousted from the management with the nomination of people's commissars by the new governments and successively either with the nationalisations which took place in those countries soon after," it said.

"The policies no longer constituted legal obligations of Generali and became the obligations of the state which expropriated Generali's business or of the state-owned company which succeeded to its liabilities," the statement added.
